Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models
papers.research_question: How to update knowledge in large language models without disrupting preserved knowledge, especially in sequential editing scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlphaEdit, a knowledge editing method that projects parameter perturbations onto the null space of preserved knowledge to avoid disrupting it during updates.
papers.conclusion: AlphaEdit is an effective and efficient method for knowledge editing that successfully updates target knowledge while preserving existing knowledge and maintaining model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
AlphaEdit improves the performance of existing locating-then-editing methods by an average of 36.7%.
AlphaEdit maintains the general capabilities of post-edited LLMs and prevents degradation in sequential editing.
AlphaEdit prevents overfitting and avoids distributional shifts in hidden representations.
AlphaEdit can be integrated into existing editing methods with a single line of code for projection, significantly boosting their performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit hallucinations due to incorrect or outdated knowledge. Hence, model editing methods have emerged to enable targeted knowledge updates. To achieve this, a prevailing paradigm is the locating-then-editing approach, which first locates influential parameters and then edits them by introducing a perturbation. While effective, current studies have demonstrated that this perturbation inevitably disrupt the originally preserved knowledge within LLMs, especially in sequential editing scenarios. To address this, we introduce AlphaEdit, a novel solution that projects perturbation onto the null space of the preserved knowledge before applying it to the parameters. We theoretically prove that this projection ensures the output of post-edited LLMs remains unchanged when queried about the preserved knowledge, thereby mitigating the issue of disruption. Extensive experiments on various LLMs, including LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, and GPT-J, show that AlphaEdit boosts the performance of most locating-then-editing methods by an average of 36.7% with a single line of additional code for projection solely. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jianghoucheng/AlphaEdit.

papers.title: Uncovering Overfitting in Large Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: Why do edited large language models perform poorly on complex tasks, and how can we mitigate the overfitting that causes this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the Editing Overfit phenomenon in knowledge editing, constructs the EVOKE benchmark for evaluation, and proposes the LTI method to mitigate overfitting by aligning the edited model's inference with in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies Editing Overfit as a key issue in knowledge editing, constructs the EVOKE benchmark for evaluation, and proposes LTI, which effectively mitigates overfitting by aligning the edited model's inference with in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Current editing methods widely lead to severe overfitting.
Locate-then-edit methods exhibit more severe overfitting to the s -> o* pattern.
Both fine-tuning based and meta-learning based methods exhibit strong overfitting to s->o* and r->o* patterns.
Norm constraints alone are insufficient to mitigate overfitting.
The proposed LTI strategy effectively mitigates Editing Overfit by aligning the edited model's inference with in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
The analysis and experiments are primarily conducted on autoregressive language models.
The LTI strategy currently relies on a simple context prefix, which may limit its effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more sophisticated context designs for LTI.
Extend the approach to other model architectures and editing scenarios.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has been proposed as an effective method for updating and correcting the internal knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing editing methods often struggle with complex tasks, such as multi-hop reasoning. In this paper, we identify and investigate the phenomenon of Editing Overfit, where edited models assign disproportionately high probabilities to the edit target, hindering the generalization of new knowledge in complex scenarios. We attribute this issue to the current editing paradigm, which places excessive emphasis on the direct correspondence between the input prompt and the edit target for each edit sample. To further explore this issue, we introduce a new benchmark, EVOKE (EValuation of Editing Overfit in Knowledge Editing), along with fine-grained evaluation metrics. Through comprehensive experiments and analysis, we demonstrate that Editing Overfit is prevalent in current editing methods and that common overfitting mitigation strategies are ineffective in knowledge editing. To overcome this, inspired by LLMs' knowledge recall mechanisms, we propose a new plug-and-play strategy called Learn the Inference (LTI), which introduce a Multi-stage Inference Constraint module to guide the edited models in recalling new knowledge similarly to how unedited LLMs leverage knowledge through in-context learning. Extensive experimental results across a wide range of tasks validate the effectiveness of LTI in mitigating Editing Overfit.

papers.title: Disentangling Knowledge Representations for Large Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we edit knowledge in large language models while effectively preserving fine-grained irrelevant knowledge (facts that share the same subject but differ in relation and object)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DiKE, a knowledge editing method that disentangles subject representations into target-related and unrelated components, enabling precise updates while preserving fine-grained irrelevant knowledge, and introduces the FINE-KED benchmark for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: DiKE effectively addresses the challenge of preserving fine-grained irrelevant knowledge during LLM editing, outperforming existing methods and maintaining strong generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) struggle to preserve fine-grained irrelevant knowledge.
DiKE significantly improves the preservation of fine-grained irrelevant knowledge across different levels of relational similarity without compromising editing efficacy.
The Knowledge Representation Disentanglement (KRD) module effectively separates target-knowledge-related and unrelated components within subject representations.
DiKE's closed-form, rank-one parameter update enables efficient and minimally invasive edits.
DiKE generalizes well to unseen subjects and relations, demonstrating the robustness of the disentanglement approach.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing has emerged as a promising solution for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). While existing approaches demonstrate effectiveness in integrating new knowledge and preserving the original capabilities of LLMs, they fail to maintain fine-grained irrelevant knowledge facts that share the same subject as edited knowledge but differ in relation and object. This challenge arises because subject representations inherently encode multiple attributes, causing the target and fine-grained irrelevant knowledge to become entangled in the representation space, and thus vulnerable to unintended alterations during editing. To address this, we propose DiKE, a novel approach that Disentangles Knowledge representations for LLM Editing (DiKE). DiKE consists of two key components: a Knowledge Representation Disentanglement (KRD) module that decomposes the subject representation into target-knowledgerelated and -unrelated components, and a Disentanglement-based Knowledge Edit (DKE) module that updates only the target-related component while explicitly preserving the unrelated one. We further derive a closed-form, rank-one parameter update based on matrix theory to enable efficient and minimally invasive edits. To rigorously evaluate fine-grained irrelevant knowledge preservation, we construct FINE-KED, a new benchmark comprising fine-grained irrelevant knowledge at different levels of relational similarity to the edited knowledge. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that DiKE substantially improves fine-grained irrelevant knowledge preservation while maintaining competitive general editing performance.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Relation Also Knows: Rethinking the Recall and Editing of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the relation (not just the subject) contribute to factual knowledge recall in auto-regressive transformer LMs, and how can knowledge editing be performed to avoid the over-generalizing problem by considering both relation and subject?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel relation-focused interpretation of factual knowledge recall in transformer LMs, showing that relational knowledge is aggregated at the last relation token, and proposes the RETS editing method which modifies the MLP at this position with subject constraints to significantly alleviate the over-generalizing problem.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel relation-focused perspective on knowledge recall in transformer LMs and demonstrates that the RETS editing method effectively avoids the over-generalizing problem, breaking the domination of subject-focused editing for future research.
papers.key_findings:
The last relation token is the decisive position for processing relation information during knowledge recall, with MLP and MHSA sublayers being most active there.
Relation-related attributes are aggregated from early to middle-late layers at the last relation token, and the target object is extracted from this aggregated relational knowledge.
Existing subject-focused editing methods (e.g., ROME) suffer from over-generalizing because they edit at the last subject token, which is earlier than the completion of relation inference and cannot attend to the relation token.
The proposed RETS method, which edits the middle-late MLP layer at the last relation token with subject constraints, outperforms baselines by over 30% on the new R-Specificity metric while remaining competitive on other criteria.
Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the subject constraints in RETS, as their removal leads to a significant drop in specificity performance.
papers.limitation:
The design of the subject constraints for RETS is relatively simple and negatively affects the quality of text generations (Fluency and Consistency).
The method is only applicable to editing each factual association separately and does not scale to sequential or batched edits.
The work only focuses on the MLP sublayers for knowledge recall, and a more complete explanation might require investigating other components.
future_direction: In-depth studies on how subject information is combined into the relation representation.
Scaling the editing method to sequential or batched facts.
Investigating other model components beyond MLP for a more complete explanation of the inference mechanism.
papers.abstract: The storage and recall of factual associations in auto-regressive transformer language models (LMs) have drawn a great deal of attention, inspiring knowledge editing by directly modifying the located model weights. Most editing works achieve knowledge editing under the guidance of existing interpretations of knowledge recall that mainly focus on subject knowledge. However, these interpretations are seriously flawed, neglecting relation information and leading to the over-generalizing problem for editing. In this work, we discover a novel relation-focused perspective to interpret the knowledge recall of transformer LMs during inference and apply it on single knowledge editing to avoid over-generalizing. Experimental results on the dataset supplemented with a new R-Specificity criterion demonstrate that our editing approach significantly alleviates over-generalizing while remaining competitive on other criteria, breaking the domination of subject-focused editing for future research.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: PropMEND: Hypernetworks for Knowledge Propagation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we improve knowledge propagation in large language models when editing knowledge, enabling them to answer multi-hop questions that require reasoning with the injected knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PropMEND, a hypernetwork-based approach that meta-learns to modify gradients of a language modeling loss to encourage injected knowledge to propagate, enabling models to answer multi-hop questions involving that knowledge.
papers.conclusion: PropMEND enables effective knowledge propagation in LLMs and outperforms existing methods, but generalization to unseen relations remains a challenge for future work.
papers.key_findings:
PropMEND achieves almost 2x accuracy on non-verbatim multi-hop questions in the RippleEdit dataset compared to the next best system.
PropMEND outperforms existing approaches on the Controlled RippleEdit dataset, both in-domain and on out-of-domain generalization, though performance degrades when relations are unseen.
The method is efficient, with similar memory and runtime to MEND when editing the same number of layers.
Ablations show that using propagation questions in the outer loop and editing mid-upper layers are key design choices.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades in out-of-domain settings, especially when relations are unseen during hypernetwork training.
future_direction: Future work in propagating knowledge to a wide range of relations.
Scaling up hypernetwork size and meta-training data to improve out-of-domain performance.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing techniques for large language models (LLMs) can inject knowledge that is later reproducible verbatim, but they fall short on propagating that knowledge: models cannot answer questions that require reasoning with the injected knowledge. We present a hypernetwork-based approach for knowledge propagation, named PropMEND, where we meta-learn how to modify gradients of a language modeling loss to encourage injected information to propagate. Our approach extends the meta-objective of MEND [29] so that gradient updates on knowledge are transformed to enable answering multi-hop questions involving that knowledge. We show improved performance on the RippleEdit dataset, showing almost 2x accuracy on challenging multi-hop questions whose answers are not explicitly stated in the injected fact. We further introduce a new dataset, Controlled RippleEdit, to evaluate the generalization of our hypernetwork, testing knowledge propagation along relations and entities unseen during hypernetwork training. PropMEND still outperforms existing approaches in unseen entity-relation pairs, yet the performance gap decreases substantially, suggesting future work in propagating knowledge to a wide range of relations.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Balancing Knowledge Updates: Toward Unified Modular Editing in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in LLMs be improved by jointly updating both MLP and Attention modules, rather than focusing solely on MLP modules?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IntAttn-Edit, a novel knowledge editing method that jointly updates both MLP and Attention modules using a knowledge balancing strategy, which proportionally allocates update magnitudes based on each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: IntAttn-Edit addresses the limitation of knowledge residuals in existing methods by jointly editing MLP and Attention modules, leading to more balanced and comprehensive knowledge updates that outperform existing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers, functioning as key-value associative memory structures.
IntAttn-Edit consistently outperforms existing editing baselines (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) on benchmarks like ZsRE and WikiData counterfact, achieving higher edit success and portability.
The proposed knowledge balancing strategy, which dynamically allocates update magnitudes between MLP and Attn modules based on their causal contributions, maintains editing performance within an optimal range.
Updating only a subset of knowledge-storage modules (e.g., only MLP) can leave residual outdated knowledge, which IntAttn-Edit mitigates by jointly editing both modules.
Extensive experiments show IntAttn-Edit delivers superior results across different batch sizes and models while maintaining high locality and fluency.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as an efficient approach for updating factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It typically locates knowledge storage modules and then modifies their parameters. However, most existing methods focus on the weights of multilayer perceptron (MLP) modules, which are often identified as the main repositories of factual information. Other components, such as attention (Attn) modules, are often ignored during editing. This imbalance can leave residual outdated knowledge and limit editing effectiveness. We perform comprehensive knowledge localization experiments on advanced LLMs and find that Attn modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers. Based on these insights, we propose IntAttn-Edit, a method that extends the associative memory paradigm to jointly update both MLP and Attn modules. Our approach uses a knowledge balancing strategy that allocates update magnitudes in proportion to each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that IntAttn-Edit achieves higher edit success, better generalization, and stronger knowledge preservation than prior methods. Further analysis shows that the balancing strategy keeps editing performance within an optimal range across diverse settings.

papers.title: AdaEdit: Advancing Continuous Knowledge Editing For Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate performance decline in the large-size continuous knowledge editing for language models?
papers.core_contribution: AdaEdit is a novel knowledge editing method that mitigates performance decline in continuous editing by disentangling representations and sparsifying perturbation weights, preserving the general abilities of edited language models.
papers.conclusion: AdaEdit effectively addresses the performance decline in continuous knowledge editing, achieving state-of-the-art edit performance while preserving the general capabilities of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Perturbation weight in continuous knowledge editing is intrinsically sparse, low-rank, and shifts from the original distribution.
Disentangling knowledge representation (using FFN-only hidden states) reduces pairwise similarity and leads to better editing performance.
Sparsifying the perturbation weight via SVD and hard-thresholding (SRFusion) mitigates parameter interference and improves performance retention in continuous editing.
AdaEdit outperforms existing baselines on standard editing datasets (ZsRE, Counterfact) in continuous editing settings.
AdaEdit maintains the general abilities (e.g., on MMLU, BBH, GSM8K) of language models after large-scale continuous edits, unlike many baseline methods.

papers.title: Beyond Local Edits: Embedding-Virtualized Knowledge for Broader Evaluation and Preservation of Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and improve the specificity of knowledge editing in large language models beyond the limitations of dataset-bounded, sample-based benchmarks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EVK-Bench, an embedding-level benchmark for broader evaluation of knowledge editing, and EVK-Align, a plug-and-play module to constrain embedding-level knowledge drift during editing, improving specificity.
papers.conclusion: EVK-Bench enables a broader, annotation-free evaluation of knowledge editing side effects, and EVK-Align provides a practical method to constrain edit propagation in embedding space, leading to more controllable model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods perform well on conventional benchmarks but show significant performance drops on the proposed EVK-Bench, indicating latent knowledge drift not captured by sample-based metrics.
The proposed EVK-Edit method (integrating EVK-Align) matches or surpasses baseline editing efficacy while consistently improving specificity and stability on both conventional benchmarks and EVK-Bench.
EVK-Align can be integrated as a plug-and-play module into various Locate-Then-Edit (LTE) algorithms, improving editing specificity with minimal impact on general language abilities.
EVK-Bench, constructed via controlled perturbations in embedding space, provides a broader and more stringent evaluation of editing specificity compared to predefined textual prompts.
Hyperparameter analysis shows that the knowledge drift strength (σ) and alignment strength (λ) are key factors controlling the trade-off between edit efficacy and specificity.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing methods for large language models are commonly evaluated using predefined benchmarks that assess edited facts together with a limited set of related or neighboring knowledge. While effective, such evaluations remain confined to finite, dataset-bounded samples, leaving the broader impact of editing on the model's knowledge system insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce Embedding-Virtualized Knowledge (EVK) that characterizes model knowledge through controlled perturbations in embedding space, enabling the exploration of a substantially broader and virtualized knowledge region beyond explicit data annotations. Based on EVK, we construct an embedding-level evaluation benchmark EVK-Bench that quantifies potential knowledge drift induced by editing, revealing effects that are not captured by conventional sample-based metrics. Furthermore, we propose a plug-and-play EVK-Align module that constrains embedding-level knowledge drift during editing and can be seamlessly integrated into existing editing methods. Experiments demonstrate that our approach enables more comprehensive evaluation while significantly improving knowledge preservation without sacrificing editing accuracy.

papers.title: Multilingual Knowledge Editing with Language-Agnostic Factual Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously edit factual knowledge across multiple languages in large language models while avoiding knowledge conflicts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LU-LAFNs, a method for multilingual knowledge editing by identifying and updating language-agnostic factual neurons in LLMs, which avoids knowledge conflicts and improves edit performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies language-agnostic factual neurons in LLMs and proposes the LU-LAFNs method for effective multilingual knowledge editing, which avoids conflicts and achieves superior performance on benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-agnostic factual neurons (LAFNs) exist in LLMs and represent factual knowledge shared across languages.
LU-LAFNs achieves the best edit performance on Bi-ZsRE and MzsRE benchmarks compared to existing methods.
The method avoids knowledge conflicts by modeling semantic connections between multilingual knowledge through shared neurons.
Edit performance is influenced by LLMs' inherent language capabilities and the selection of layers for updating.
Using paraphrases during the locating stage improves edit performance by precisely identifying relevant neurons.
papers.limitation:
Requires aligned multilingual knowledge and subjects, which may need preprocessing if not available in datasets.
Exact-match for cache subject matching is too strict and will be optimized to fuzzy matching in future work.
Poor performance on the Portability metric, indicating limited reasoning ability based on edited knowledge.
future_direction: Optimize cache subject matching to a fuzzy matching method.
Improve the method for reasoning scenarios, such as testing on the CROLIN-MQUAKE benchmark.
papers.abstract: Multilingual knowledge editing (MKE) aims to simultaneously update factual knowledge across multiple languages within large language models (LLMs). Previous research indicates that the same knowledge across different languages within LLMs exhibits a degree of shareability. However, most existing MKE methods overlook the connections of the same knowledge between different languages, resulting in knowledge conflicts and limited edit performance. To address this issue, we first investigate how LLMs process multilingual factual knowledge and discover that the same factual knowledge in different languages generally activates a shared set of neurons, which we call language-agnostic factual neurons (LAFNs). These neurons represent the same factual knowledge shared across languages and imply the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge. Inspired by this finding, we propose a new MKE method by Locating and Updating Language-Agnostic Factual Neurons (LU-LAFNs) to edit multilingual knowledge simultaneously, which avoids knowledge conflicts and thus improves edit performance. Experimental results on Bi-ZsRE and MzsRE benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves the best edit performance, indicating the effectiveness and importance of modeling the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Unlocking Efficient, Scalable, and Continual Knowledge Editing with Basis-Level Representation Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Are the editing-locality trade-offs in knowledge editing caused by the global effect of parameter-based updates? Can representation fine-tuning provide a better solution?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BaFT, a basis-level representation fine-tuning method for knowledge editing that uses input-dependent weighting to achieve a better editing-locality trade-off than previous methods.
papers.conclusion: BaFT is an effective representation fine-tuning method for knowledge editing that achieves a better editing-locality trade-off and maintains parameter efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
BaFT achieves competitive editing performance with better locality than ReFT and other baselines.
BaFT generalizes ReFT and allows fine-grained control over updates.
BaFT is parameter-efficient, using fewer parameters than methods like WISE.
BaFT works well in single, continual, and batched editing scenarios.
Theoretical analysis shows linear representation fine-tuning has an inherent editing-locality trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Empirical success on standard benchmarks may not reflect diverse real-world applications.
Requires hyper-parameter tuning to determine proper positions and layers to add interventions.
It is unknown if representation-based methods can fit any editing learnable by parameter-based methods.
future_direction: Explore automating the process by imposing sparsity constraints on weights.
Investigate if representation-based methods can fit any editing learnable by parameter-based methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on various natural language tasks. However, they are trained on static corpora and their knowledge can become outdated quickly in the fast-changing world. This motivates the development of knowledge editing methods designed to update certain knowledge in LLMs without changing unrelated others. To make selective edits, previous efforts often sought to update a small amount of parameters in some specific layer(s) of a LLM. Nonetheless, in challenging scenarios, they still fall short in making successful edits while preserving knowledge irrelevant to the updates simultaneously, resulting in a notable editing-locality trade-off. In this work, we question if the trade-offs are caused by the fact that parameter-based updates have a global effect, i.e., edited parameters affect all inputs indiscriminately. In light of this, we explore the feasibility of representation fine-tuning, which applied some linear update to a few representations in a learned subspace, for knowledge editing. While being effective to enhance an LLM's general ability as demonstrated in the previous work, we theoretically show that this linear update imposes a tension in editing-locality trade-off. Subsequently, BaFT is proposed to break the linearity. BaFT computes a weight for each basis that spans a dimension of the subspace based on the input representation. This input-dependent weighting mechanism allows BaFT to manage different types of knowledge in an adaptive way, thereby achieving a better editing-locality trade-off. Experiments on three LLMs with five editing benchmarks in diverse scenarios show the superiority of our method.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: MoEEdit: Efficient and Routing-Stable Knowledge Editing for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.research_question: How to perform efficient and routing-stable knowledge editing in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MoEEdit, a routing-stable knowledge editing framework for MoE LLMs that uses per-expert null-space projection to suppress routing shifts and a block coordinate descent solver for efficient updates.
papers.conclusion: MoEEdit establishes a robust foundation for precise and scalable knowledge editing in sparse MoE architectures, highlighting the importance of expert-aware, routing-stable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
MoEEdit achieves state-of-the-art efficacy, generalization, and specificity on COUNTERFACT and zsRE benchmarks.
MoEEdit maintains high routing stability (routing similarity) compared to baseline methods.
The per-expert null-space projection is critical for suppressing routing distribution shift.
The block coordinate descent solver scales efficiently with the number of experts.
MoEEdit outperforms adapted dense-model editing methods on MoE LLMs.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing (KE) enables precise modifications to factual content in large language models (LLMs). Existing KE methods are largely designed for dense architectures, limiting their applicability to the increasingly prevalent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that underpin modern scalable LLMs. Although MoEs offer strong efficiency and capacity scaling, naively adapting dense-model editors is both computationally costly and prone to routing distribution shifts that undermine stability and consistency. To address these challenges, we introduce MoEEdit, the first routing-stable framework for parameter-modifying knowledge editing in MoE LLMs. Our method reparameterizes expert updates via per-expert null-space projections that keep router inputs invariant and thereby suppress routing shifts. The resulting block-structured optimization is solved efficiently with a block coordinate descent (BCD) solver. Experiments show that MoEEdit attains state-of-the-art efficacy and generalization while preserving high specificity and routing stability, with superior compute and memory efficiency. These results establish a robust foundation for scalable, precise knowledge editing in sparse LLMs and underscore the importance of routing-stable interventions.

papers.title: StruEdit: Structured Outputs Enable the Fast and Accurate Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing for large language models be made more accurate and efficient by using structured outputs to avoid the challenges of locating and editing within natural language reasoning steps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STRUEDIT, a knowledge editing method that removes parametric knowledge and refills structured reasoning triplets with updated information, enabling fast and accurate multi-hop editing without needing to locate specific tokens or parameters.
papers.conclusion: STRUEDIT offers a new paradigm for knowledge editing with higher accuracy, faster performance, and greater robustness, paving the way for further advancements in the field.
papers.key_findings:
STRUEDIT consistently achieves the highest editing accuracy and lowest latency compared to existing model editing and in-context editing methods.
STRUEDIT shows robust performance as the number of reasoning hops and edited instances increases, with a smaller performance drop than other methods.
The method does not require locating specific knowledge to edit, instead removing all potentially affected parametric knowledge and reasoning over updated knowledge structures.
STRUEDIT's performance advantage is more pronounced on smaller open-source models, indicating it reduces the burden on LLMs' inherent capabilities.
Existing knowledge editing methods suffer from performance degradation due to knowledge conflicts and hallucinations during multi-hop reasoning, which STRUEDIT mitigates.
papers.limitation:
STRUEDIT requires a more structured knowledge format (like knowledge graphs) to support LLM reasoning, unlike text-based editing information used by other methods.
There is a noticeable decline in performance as reasoning hops and the number of edited instances increase, indicating potential errors in LLM reasoning during entity and relation extraction.
papers.abstract: As the modern tool of choice for question answering, large language models (LLMs) are expected to deliver answers with up-to-date knowledge. To achieve such ideal question-answering systems, locating and then editing outdated knowledge in the natural language outputs is a general target of popular knowledge editing methods. However, this target is challenging, as both identifying which tokens to edit in the reasoning steps and ensuring the coherence of the revised reasoning chain are difficult tasks. We argue that these challenges stem from the unstructured nature of natural language outputs. To address the above challenges, we propose $\textbf{Stru}$ctural $\textbf{Edit}$ing ($\textbf{StruEdit}$), an improved baseline for knowledge editing. We first prompt LLMs to produce structured outputs consisting of reasoning triplets. Then, StruEdit removes any potentially outdated knowledge and efficiently refills the structured outputs with up-to-date information in a single step. Experimental results show that StruEdit consistently delivers the highest accuracy with lowest latency compared with other knowledge editing methods.

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Surgical Knowledge Rewrite in Compact LLMs: An 'Unlearn-then-Learn' Strategy with ($IA^3$) for Localized Factual Modulation and Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
papers.research_question: How to achieve precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs for conflicting factual updates while mitigating catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mechanistically informed 'unlearn-then-learn' strategy with IA3 that achieves precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs, with high accuracy for new facts and minimal catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The method enables deterministic, precise, and localized knowledge editing, advancing LLM knowledge management with enhanced safety and control.
papers.key_findings:
Achieves 98.50% accuracy for the new fact and 96.00% forget rate for the original fact.
Shows 72.00% F_control accuracy, significantly mitigating catastrophic forgetting compared to direct fine-tuning.
Demonstrates 'soft forgetting' where original knowledge is suppressed but remains latently accessible.
Outperforms direct fine-tuning methods like LoRA and IA3 in localization and fact modulation.
Uses circuit localization to inform targeted PEFT application for effective editing.
papers.limitation: The method may struggle to scale with sequential unlearning requests or larger forget sets in very large LLMs.
future_direction: Scalability of the strategy to larger LLMs
Further mechanistic insights into 'soft forgetting' and auditing unlearning
Potential for multi-fact and chained knowledge edits
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with dynamic knowledge updates, especially when new information conflicts with deeply embedded facts. Such conflicting factual edits often lead to two critical issues: resistance to adopting the new fact and severe catastrophic forgetting of unrelated knowledge. This paper introduces and evaluates a novel "unlearn-then-learn" strategy for precise knowledge editing in LLMs, leveraging the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique, Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations ($IA^3$). Crucially, this two-stage approach is powered by an initial circuit localization phase that identifies and targets the specific internal components responsible for encoding the conflicting fact. Through a rigorous experimental methodology on microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, we demonstrate that this mechanistically informed two-stage approach achieves near-perfect accuracy (98.50%) for the new, modulated fact while simultaneously effectively suppressing the original conflicting fact (96.00% forget rate). Critically, our strategy exhibits unprecedented localization (72.00% F_control accuracy), dramatically mitigating catastrophic forgetting observed in direct fine-tuning approaches (which showed as low as ~20% F_control accuracy), a direct benefit of our targeted interpretability-guided intervention. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals a nuanced mechanism of "soft forgetting," where original knowledge is suppressed from default retrieval but remains latent and conditionally accessible, enhancing model safety and control. These findings represent a significant advancement towards precise, localized, and safe knowledge management in compact LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unlearning: Robust Knowledge Unlearning and Editing via Mechanistic Localization
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability improve the precision and effectiveness of knowledge editing and unlearning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic unlearning, which localizes edits to fact lookup mechanisms, improves robustness in knowledge editing and unlearning across different prompts and resists relearning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic unlearning via FLU localization provides a robust framework for knowledge editing and unlearning, outperforming output-tracing methods.
papers.key_findings:
FLU localization leads to more robust edits/unlearning across different input/output formats compared to output-tracing methods.
FLU localization resists attempts to relearn the unwanted information, making unlearning more persistent.
FLU localization reduces unintended side effects on general language modeling capabilities compared to baselines.
FLU localization modifies internal latent knowledge to reflect edited answers more effectively than other methods.
Output-tracing methods target extraction mechanisms rather than fact lookup, leading to less robust edits.
papers.abstract: Methods for knowledge editing and unlearning in large language models seek to edit or remove undesirable knowledge or capabilities without compromising general language modeling performance. This work investigates how mechanistic interpretability -- which, in part, aims to identify model components (circuits) associated to specific interpretable mechanisms that make up a model capability -- can improve the precision and effectiveness of editing and unlearning. We find a stark difference in unlearning and edit robustness when training components localized by different methods. We highlight an important distinction between methods that localize components based primarily on preserving outputs, and those finding high level mechanisms with predictable intermediate states. In particular, localizing edits/unlearning to components associated with the lookup-table mechanism for factual recall 1) leads to more robust edits/unlearning across different input/output formats, and 2) resists attempts to relearn the unwanted information, while also reducing unintended side effects compared to baselines, on both a sports facts dataset and the CounterFact dataset across multiple models. We also find that certain localized edits disrupt the latent knowledge in the model more than any other baselines, making unlearning more robust to various attacks.

papers.title: Dynamic Contextual Alignment Mechanisms for Improving the Internal Representational Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to improve internal representational consistency in large language models by aligning intermediate representations across layers and attention heads.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic Contextual Alignment Mechanisms, a framework that dynamically aligns intermediate representations across layers to improve contextual coherence and reduce ambiguities in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic Contextual Alignment Mechanisms effectively improve internal representational consistency in LLMs, enhancing contextual coherence and reducing semantic ambiguities with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
The mechanism reduces perplexity by 22.2% and average attention entropy by 16.7%, indicating improved contextual understanding.
Layer-wise consistency scores increase by 23.6%, demonstrating enhanced representational alignment across model layers.
Accuracy in handling long-range dependencies improves consistently, with gains over baseline models for dependency lengths up to 250 tokens.
The framework shows superior robustness to input noise, maintaining higher accuracy levels under varying noise conditions.
Adaptability across diverse domains (legal, medical, technical) is demonstrated with improved performance scores.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on recalibration layers introduces additional parameters, which could present scalability challenges for extremely large models.
The mechanism's reliance on attention weight adjustments may be limited when input structures deviate from pre-training distributions.
future_direction: Integrating more robust noise-handling components
Exploring hybrid strategies that combine contextual recalibration with external knowledge
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of language models naturally demands innovative approaches to maintain internal representational consistency. This paper introduces Dynamic Contextual Alignment Mechanisms, a novel framework designed to enhance semantic coherence within large language models. By integrating adaptive recalibration strategies, the proposed mechanism aligns intermediate representations across multiple layers, thereby reducing contextual ambiguities and improving the interpretative processes of language models. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate significant reductions in perplexity and attention entropy, alongside improvements in coherence scores, indicating the mechanism's efficacy in refining contextual understanding. Comparative analyses reveal that, unlike traditional methods relying on fine-tuning or auxiliary layers, this approach inherently enhances alignment without substantial computational overhead. The findings demonstrate the potential of Dynamic Contextual Alignment Mechanisms to advance the robustness and adaptability of language models across diverse applications, addressing fundamental challenges in representational alignment and setting a foundation for future developments in the field.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Interference in Multilingual Knowledge Editing through Null-Space Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently update knowledge in multilingual large language models sequentially across languages without causing negative interference and while preserving multilingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LangEdit, a null-space constrained framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that projects parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: LangEdit is an effective framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that uses null-space projection to isolate language-specific updates, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization, as demonstrated across multiple models and languages.
papers.key_findings:
LangEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in multilingual sequential knowledge editing, improving editing accuracy and multilingual generalization across three model architectures and six languages.
LangEdit effectively mitigates negative interference by projecting language-specific updates onto the null space of previous updates, preserving performance in previously edited languages.
The method demonstrates cross-lingual knowledge transfer, where edits in one language can be accessed in another without explicit editing in that language.
Editing effectiveness varies by language, with languages having less pretraining data (e.g., Spanish) showing greater improvement than high-resource languages (e.g., English).
LangEdit maintains high specificity, ensuring that edits do not affect unrelated knowledge, and improves downstream task performance on multilingual benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on 6-8B parameter LLMs; extending to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) could reveal scaling effects.
The current evaluation focuses on constrained editing scenarios; future work should explore a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Multilingual experiments are limited to 6 languages; developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages would better test the boundaries of LangEdit and baselines.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) to reveal scaling effects.
Exploring a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages.
papers.abstract: Efficiently updating multilingual knowledge in large language models (LLMs), while preserving consistent factual representations across languages, remains a long-standing and unresolved challenge.While deploying separate editing systems for each language might seem viable, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the need to manage multiple models.A more efficient solution involves integrating knowledge updates across all languages into a unified model.However, performing sequential edits across languages often leads to destructive parameter interference, significantly degrading multilingual generalization and the accuracy of injected knowledge.To address this challenge, we propose LangEdit, a novel null-space constrained framework designed to precisely isolate language-specific knowledge updates.The core innovation of LangEdit lies in its ability to project parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces.This approach mathematically guarantees update independence while preserving multilingual generalization capabilities.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across three model architectures, six languages, and four downstream tasks, demonstrating that LangEdit effectively mitigates parameter interference and outperforms existing state-of-the-art editing methods.Our results highlight its potential for enabling efficient and accurate multilingual knowledge updates in LLMs.The code is available at https: //github.com/VRCMF/LangEdit.git.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
