papers.limitation: The study is not exhaustive across different types of models or datasets used.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of localized updates to large language models (LLMs), specifically in the context of knowledge editing - a task aimed at incorporating or modifying specific facts without altering broader model capabilities. We first show that across different post-training interventions like continuous pre-training, full fine-tuning and LORA-based fine-tuning, the Frobenius norm of the updated matrices always increases. This increasing norm is especially detrimental for localized knowledge editing, where only a subset of matrices are updated in a model . We reveal a consistent phenomenon across various editing techniques, including fine-tuning, hypernetwork-based approaches, and locate-and-edit methods: the norm of the updated matrix invariably increases with successive updates. Such growth disrupts model balance, particularly when isolated matrices are updated while the rest of the model remains static, leading to potential instability and degradation of downstream performance. Upon deeper investigations of the intermediate activation vectors, we find that the norm of internal activations decreases and is accompanied by shifts in the subspaces occupied by these activations, which shows that these activation vectors now occupy completely different regions in the representation space compared to the unedited model. With our paper, we highlight the technical challenges with continuous and localized sequential knowledge editing and their implications for maintaining model stability and utility.

papers.title: A Dual-Axis Taxonomy of Knowledge Editing for LLMs: From Mechanisms to Functions
papers.core_contribution: This survey introduces a novel function-based taxonomy for knowledge editing in LLMs, complementing existing mechanism-based taxonomies, to provide a more holistic view of the field.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing is an efficient alternative to retraining for updating LLMs, and this survey provides a comprehensive review by analyzing the field along mechanism and function axes, highlighting future challenges for adaptive, scalable, and secure editors.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing methods can be categorized into parameter-modifying and parameter-preserving mechanisms.
The effectiveness of an editing method depends on the type of knowledge being edited (factual, temporal, conceptual, commonsense, social).
Current methods are primarily designed for factual knowledge and struggle with more complex knowledge types like commonsense and social knowledge.
There is a trade-off between locality and generalization in knowledge editing.
The field lacks theoretical foundations and faces challenges in scalability and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The survey represents a snapshot of research primarily published by mid-2025 and may not include very recent work.
The survey prioritizes categorization and synthesis over deep technical analysis of every individual method.
The survey does not provide a detailed comparison with related fields such as continual learning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
The survey does not introduce new empirical results or perform controlled, head-to-head comparisons of methods.
future_direction: Towards optimization-free and runtime editing.
Automating the discovery of knowledge to edit.
Enhancing robustness and security of edited models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire vast knowledge from large text corpora, but this information can become outdated or inaccurate. Since retraining is computationally expensive, knowledge editing offers an efficient alternative -- modifying internal knowledge without full retraining. These methods aim to update facts precisely while preserving the model's overall capabilities. While existing surveys focus on the mechanism of editing (e.g., parameter changes vs. external memory), they often overlook the function of the knowledge being edited. This survey introduces a novel, complementary function-based taxonomy to provide a more holistic view. We examine how different mechanisms apply to various knowledge types -- factual, temporal, conceptual, commonsense, and social -- highlighting how editing effectiveness depends on the nature of the target knowledge. By organizing our review along these two axes, we map the current landscape, outline the strengths and limitations of existing methods, define the problem formally, survey evaluation tasks and datasets, and conclude with open challenges and future directions.

papers.title: History Matters: Temporal Knowledge Editing in Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we edit temporal knowledge in large language models to update outdated information while preserving historical knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Temporal Knowledge Editing (TKE) task and the ATOKE benchmark, and proposes the METO framework to enhance existing knowledge editing methods by preserving historical knowledge while learning new knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Temporal Knowledge Editing remains a challenging task, but the METO framework improves existing methods; further community effort is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods cause catastrophic forgetting of historical knowledge when updating temporal facts.
Relative time questions (e.g., 'previous') are more difficult for edited models than explicit time questions.
Performance degrades with multiple consecutive edits on the same fact.
Extending the time scope of a fact is easier for models than inserting a new object.
The proposed METO framework significantly improves historical knowledge preservation while maintaining effectiveness on new knowledge.
future_direction: Further research on temporal knowledge editing.
papers.abstract: The imperative task of revising or updating the knowledge stored within large language models arises from two distinct sources: intrinsic errors inherent in the model which should be corrected and outdated knowledge due to external shifts in the real world which should be updated. Prevailing efforts in model editing conflate these two distinct categories of edits arising from distinct reasons and directly modify the original knowledge in models into new knowledge. However, we argue that preserving the model's original knowledge remains pertinent. Specifically, if a model's knowledge becomes outdated due to evolving worldly dynamics, it should retain recollection of the historical knowledge while integrating the newfound knowledge. In this work, we introduce the task of Temporal Knowledge Editing (TKE) and establish a benchmark AToKe (Assessment of TempOral Knowledge Editing) to evaluate current model editing methods. We find that while existing model editing methods are effective at making models remember new knowledge, the edited model catastrophically forgets historical knowledge. To address this gap, we propose a simple and general framework termed Multi-Editing with Time Objective (METO) for enhancing existing editing models, which edits both historical and new knowledge concurrently and optimizes the model's prediction for the time of each fact. Our assessments demonstrate that while AToKe is still difficult, METO maintains the effectiveness of learning new knowledge and meanwhile substantially improves the performance of edited models on utilizing historical knowledge.

papers.title: Enhancing Multi-hop Reasoning through Knowledge Erasure in Large Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: What is the impact of residual old knowledge on multi-hop reasoning in edited large language models, and how can knowledge erasure improve it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes KELE, a knowledge editing method that incorporates a knowledge erasure mechanism to eliminate residual old knowledge, thereby enhancing the multi-hop reasoning capability of edited large language models.
papers.conclusion: KELE is an effective knowledge editing method that enhances multi-hop reasoning by erasing residual old knowledge during the editing process.
papers.key_findings:
KELE significantly improves multi-hop accuracy compared to state-of-the-art editing methods like ROME and MEMIT.
Residual old knowledge in edited models causes them to revert to original answers in multi-hop questions, undermining performance.
Erasing old knowledge during editing reduces the likelihood of generating original answers and improves correct answer accuracy.
The degree of knowledge erasure (controlled by hyperparameter k) affects performance, with optimal values balancing erasure and model stability.
KELE effectively reduces the Retain Score, indicating successful erasure of old knowledge without harming single-hop recall.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face challenges with internal knowledge inaccuracies and outdated information. Knowledge editing has emerged as a pivotal approach to mitigate these issues. Although current knowledge editing techniques exhibit promising performance in single-hop reasoning tasks, they show limitations when applied to multi-hop reasoning. Drawing on cognitive neuroscience and the operational mechanisms of LLMs, we hypothesize that the residual single-hop knowledge after editing causes edited models to revert to their original answers when processing multi-hop questions, thereby undermining their performance in multihop reasoning tasks. To validate this hypothesis, we conduct a series of experiments that empirically confirm our assumptions. Building on the validated hypothesis, we propose a novel knowledge editing method that incorporates a Knowledge Erasure mechanism for Large language model Editing (KELE). Specifically, we design an erasure function for residual knowledge and an injection function for new knowledge. Through joint optimization, we derive the optimal recall vector, which is subsequently utilized within a rank-one editing framework to update the parameters of targeted model layers. Extensive experiments on GPT-J and GPT-2 XL demonstrate that KELE substantially enhances the multi-hop reasoning capability of edited LLMs.

papers.title: Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we improve the locality of knowledge editing in LLMs by moving from causal tracing to neuron-level localization?
papers.core_contribution: FiNE is a neuron-level knowledge editing method that improves editing locality by precisely identifying and modifying neurons in FFNs, overcoming the over-reliance on subject entities in previous causal tracing methods.
papers.conclusion: FiNE advances knowledge localization and editing in LLMs by providing a neuron-level approach that improves locality and efficiency, paving the way for more reliable knowledge management.
papers.key_findings:
Existing locate-then-edit methods based on causal tracing are overly subject-driven and neglect relations, leading to poor editing locality.
FiNE's neuron-level localization provides more precise knowledge localization than causal tracing.
FiNE achieves better locality scores and efficiency compared to existing methods like ROME, MEMIT, and PMET.
FiNE maintains high edit success and portability while significantly improving locality.
Ablation studies show that neuron localization and layer freezing are important components of FiNE.
papers.limitation: The safety of edits cannot be ensured, and there is potential for misuse such as introducing malicious misinformation or bias.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated information in Large Language Models (LLMs). A representative line of study is locate-then-edit methods, which typically employ causal tracing to identify the modules responsible for recalling factual knowledge about entities. However, we find these methods are often sensitive only to changes in the subject entity, leaving them less effective at adapting to changes in relations. This limitation results in poor editing locality, which can lead to the persistence of irrelevant or inaccurate facts, ultimately compromising the reliability of LLMs. We believe this issue arises from the insufficient precision of knowledge localization. To address this, we propose a Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing (FiNE) method that enhances editing locality without affecting overall success rates. By precisely identifying and modifying specific neurons within feed-forward networks, FiNE significantly improves knowledge localization and editing. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that FiNE efficiently achieves better overall performance compared to existing techniques, providing new insights into the localization and modification of knowledge within LLMs.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Rethinking Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do knowledge editing methods perform in practice-oriented settings, including autoregressive inference and sequential editing? Can they help reasoning LLMs integrate new facts without degrading reasoning ability, and generalize from factual to event knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive benchmarking study of knowledge editing methods, revealing that parameter-based editing methods perform poorly under realistic conditions (autoregressive inference, sequential editing), while a simple context-based baseline (SCR) consistently outperforms them.
papers.conclusion: Parameter-based knowledge editing methods have critical limitations in practical scenarios, while context-based reasoning approaches like SCR offer a more robust and promising alternative for updating knowledge in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter-modification-based knowledge editing methods exhibit poor transferability and lose multi-hop reasoning capabilities under realistic evaluation settings.
As the number of edits increases, the performance of parameter-modification methods degrades sharply, making them impractical for real-world use.
After editing, LLMs often suffer significant declines in general performance, including loss of basic reasoning and processing abilities.
In-context learning and external memory methods (like SCR) demonstrate greater stability and robustness across editing scenarios.
Most parameter-modification methods struggle to handle complex event-level knowledge, while context-based methods generalize better.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update the embedded knowledge within Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing approaches, whether through parameter modification or external memory integration, often suffer from inconsistent evaluation objectives and experimental setups. To address this gap, we conduct a comprehensive benchmarking study. In addition to fact-level datasets, we introduce more complex event-based datasets and general-purpose datasets drawn from other tasks. Our evaluation covers both instruction-tuned and reasoning-oriented LLMs, under a realistic autoregressive inference setting rather than teacher-forced decoding. Beyond single-edit assessments, we also evaluate multi-edit scenarios to better reflect practical demands. We employ four evaluation dimensions, including portability, and compare all recent methods against a simple and straightforward baseline named Selective Contextual Reasoning (SCR). Empirical results reveal that parameter-based editing methods perform poorly under realistic conditions. In contrast, SCR consistently outperforms them across all settings. This study offers new insights into the limitations of current knowledge editing methods and highlights the potential of context-based reasoning as a more robust alternative.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: REACT: Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning to Overcome Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How to overcome overfitting in LLM knowledge editing by precisely and controllably editing knowledge without overfitting to the edit target.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REACT, a two-phase framework for knowledge editing that extracts a belief-shift vector and applies controllable perturbations to hidden states, reducing overfitting while maintaining balanced editing performance.
papers.conclusion: REACT provides a practical framework for controlled knowledge editing, reducing overfitting and generalizing well, and points towards refining LLM editing without heavy parameter tuning.
papers.key_findings:
REACT achieves balanced performance across reliability, locality, and generality, outperforming baselines by at least 20 percentage points on average.
REACT shows high portability, indicating robust knowledge editing and resilience against overfitting.
REACT significantly reduces overfitting, as evidenced by lower Direct Probability scores and high Editing Overfit Scores on EVOKE.
REACT exhibits balanced calibration in Correct Answer Probability, avoiding overconfident updates.
REACT generalizes well across benchmarks, despite being trained only on COUNTERFACT.
papers.limitation:
Achieving the best possible performance typically requires fine-tuning or retraining on the specific dataset relevant to the task.
Further investigation is required to understand how edits influence broader linguistic abilities, including nuanced semantic understanding and language generation coherence.
papers.abstract: Large language model editing methods frequently suffer from overfitting, wherein factual updates can propagate beyond their intended scope, overemphasizing the edited target even when it's contextually inappropriate. To address this challenge, we introduce REACT (Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning), a unified two-phase framework designed for precise and controllable knowledge editing. In the initial phase, we utilize tailored stimuli to extract latent factual representations and apply Principal Component Analysis with a simple learnbale linear transformation to compute a directional "belief shift" vector for each instance. In the second phase, we apply controllable perturbations to hidden states using the obtained vector with a magnitude scalar, gated by a pre-trained classifier that permits edits only when contextually necessary. Relevant experiments on EVOKE benchmarks demonstrate that REACT significantly reduces overfitting across nearly all evaluation metrics, and experiments on COUNTERFACT and MQuAKE shows that our method preserves balanced basic editing performance (reliability, locality, and generality) under diverse editing scenarios.

papers.title: Neighboring Perturbations of Knowledge Editing on Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does updating new knowledge to LLMs (specifically, appending a new answer into an answer list to a factual question) perturb the neighboring knowledge, leading to catastrophic forgetting of original correct answers and unintentional inclusion of incorrect answers?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of neighboring perturbations in knowledge editing, proposes a new metric (additivity) and benchmark (PEAK) to evaluate it, and presents a plug-and-play framework (APP) to mitigate such perturbations when appending new knowledge to LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neighboring perturbations are a serious issue in knowledge editing for LLMs, and the proposed APP framework provides an effective way to mitigate these perturbations while appending new knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, MEND, ROME, MEMIT) effectively incorporate new facts but significantly perturb the probability distribution of neighboring knowledge, causing forgetting of original correct answers and introduction of false answers.
The proposed APP framework, when coupled with existing editing methods, effectively mitigates neighboring perturbations while largely maintaining the efficacy of appending new knowledge.
Larger LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-2 13B) suffer more severe neighboring perturbations after editing compared to smaller models.
Perturbations are more pronounced for false answers that are semantically close (Hard setting) to the newly appended answer compared to distant ones (Random setting).
The PEAK-T dataset (temporal edits) is more challenging for editing methods to append knowledge without perturbation compared to the counterfactual PEAK-CF dataset.
papers.abstract: Despite their exceptional capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are prone to generating unintended text due to false or outdated knowledge. Given the resource-intensive nature of retraining LLMs, there has been a notable increase in the development of knowledge editing. However, current approaches and evaluations rarely explore the perturbation of editing on neighboring knowledge. This paper studies whether updating new knowledge to LLMs perturbs the neighboring knowledge encapsulated within them. Specifically, we seek to figure out whether appending a new answer into an answer list to a factual question leads to catastrophic forgetting of original correct answers in this list, as well as unintentional inclusion of incorrect answers. A metric of additivity is introduced and a benchmark dubbed as Perturbation Evaluation of Appending Knowledge (PEAK) is constructed to evaluate the degree of perturbation to neighboring knowledge when appending new knowledge. Besides, a plug-and-play framework termed Appending via Preservation and Prevention (APP) is proposed to mitigate the neighboring perturbation by maintaining the integrity of the answer list. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of APP coupling with four editing methods on four LLMs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/mjy1111/PEAK.

papers.title: Investigating Multi-Hop Factual Shortcuts in Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the possibilities for LLMs to utilize factual shortcuts based on direct connections between initial and terminal entities in multi-hop knowledge, and what risks do these shortcuts pose in knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates multi-hop factual shortcuts in LLMs, finding that shortcuts correlate with entity co-occurrence frequency in pre-training corpora and contribute to knowledge editing failures, and proposes erasing shortcut neurons to mitigate these risks.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that factual shortcuts compromise the reasoning consistency of LLMs in knowledge editing, and while erasing neurons mitigates risks, fundamental elimination requires changes during pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Factual shortcuts exist in LLMs for multi-hop knowledge, and their strength is highly correlated with the frequency of co-occurrence of initial and terminal entities in pre-training corpora.
Few-shot prompting leverages more shortcuts in answering multi-hop questions compared to chain-of-thought prompting.
Approximately 20% of failures in multi-hop knowledge editing are attributed to factual shortcuts.
Shortcut failure instances have higher co-occurrence frequencies of initial and terminal entities in the pre-training corpus.
Erasing crucial neurons associated with factual shortcuts reduces the failure rate of multi-hop knowledge editing caused by shortcuts.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on the MQUAKE-CF-3K dataset, which may not generalize to other datasets.
Erasing shortcuts is a mitigative measure and cannot completely eliminate them; fundamental elimination requires pre-training changes.
Experiments are limited to GPT-J and LLaMA-2, not covering all publicly accessible LLMs.
future_direction: Extend statistical analyses to more expansive corpora.
Conduct comprehensive experiments on a broader spectrum of LLMs.
Address the elimination of factual shortcuts during the pre-training phase.
papers.abstract: Recent work has showcased the powerful capability of large language models (LLMs) in recalling knowledge and reasoning. However, the reliability of LLMs in combining these two capabilities into reasoning through multi-hop facts has not been widely explored. This paper systematically investigates the possibilities for LLMs to utilize shortcuts based on direct connections between the initial and terminal entities of multi-hop knowledge. We first explore the existence of factual shortcuts through Knowledge Neurons, revealing that: (i) the strength of factual shortcuts is highly correlated with the frequency of co-occurrence of initial and terminal entities in the pre-training corpora; (ii) few-shot prompting leverage more shortcuts in answering multi-hop questions compared to chain-of-thought prompting. Then, we analyze the risks posed by factual shortcuts from the perspective of multi-hop knowledge editing. Analysis shows that approximately 20% of the failures are attributed to shortcuts, and the initial and terminal entities in these failure instances usually have higher co-occurrences in the pre-training corpus. Finally, we propose erasing shortcut neurons to mitigate the associated risks and find that this approach significantly reduces failures in multiple-hop knowledge editing caused by shortcuts.

papers.title: Locate-then-edit for Multi-hop Factual Recall under Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Why do existing locate-then-edit knowledge editing methods fail on multi-hop factual recall tasks, and how can they be improved by editing both shallow and deep MLP layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that in multi-hop tasks, LLMs retrieve knowledge from deeper MLP layers, unlike single-hop tasks, and proposes IFMET, a locate-then-edit method that edits both shallow and deep layers using multi-hop prompts, significantly improving multi-hop factual recall.
papers.conclusion: IFMET effectively edits knowledge in both shallow and deep MLP layers, overcoming limitations of previous methods and leading to significant improvements in multi-hop factual recall tasks.
papers.key_findings:
In multi-hop scenarios, implicit subject information accumulates before the final answer at the last token position, unlike single-hop where subject is explicit.
The implicit subject has causal effects on the final answer in multi-hop reasoning, as shown by intervention experiments.
Knowledge is retrieved from deeper MLP layers in multi-hop tasks, while from shallow layers in single-hop.
Existing locate-then-edit methods fail on multi-hop tasks because they only edit shallow layers, leaving deeper layers unchanged.
IFMET successfully edits both shallow and deep MLP layers using single-hop and multi-hop prompts, improving multi-hop accuracy.
papers.abstract: The locate-then-edit paradigm has shown significant promise for knowledge editing (KE) in Large Language Models (LLMs). While previous methods perform well on single-hop fact recall tasks, they consistently struggle with multi-hop factual recall tasks involving newly edited knowledge. In this paper, leveraging tools in mechanistic interpretability, we first identify that in multi-hop tasks, LLMs tend to retrieve knowledge with implicit subject information from deeper MLP layers, unlike single-hop tasks, which rely on shallow layers. This distinction explains the poor performance of current methods in multi-hop queries, as they primarily focus on editing shallow layers with single-hop edit prompts, leaving deeper layers unchanged. To address this, we propose IFMET, a novel locate-then-edit KE approach designed to edit both shallow and deep MLP layers. Beyond single-hop editing prompts, IFMET further incorporates multi-hop editing prompts to locate and modify knowledge across different stages of reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that IFMET significantly improves performance on multi-hop factual recall tasks, overcoming the limitations of previous locate-then-edit methods

papers.title: MQuAKE: Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Multi-Hop Questions
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing methods correctly answer multi-hop questions that are entailed consequences of edited facts, beyond simply recalling the edited facts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MQUAKE, a benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing methods via multi-hop questions, and proposes MeLLo, a memory-based editing method that outperforms existing approaches.
papers.conclusion: Current knowledge editing methods are not faithful in handling multi-hop questions, and MeLLo is proposed as an effective alternative that outperforms existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods fail catastrophically on multi-hop questions despite performing well on single-hop recall.
MeLLo significantly outperforms existing knowledge editing methods on multi-hop questions.
MeLLo scales well to large language models like GPT-3 and does not require weight updates.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves multi-hop performance but still leaves a large gap for edited models.
When editing more facts at scale, multi-hop performance drops further for existing methods.
papers.limitation:
Mainly evaluate on GPT-J and Vicuna-7B, leaving evaluation on other LLMs for future work.
MeLLo relies on language models for question decomposition and self-checking, and its performance with smaller models like GPT-2 is not studied.
MeLLo requires manually defined prompts for new tasks.
future_direction: Evaluate knowledge editing methods on other LLMs beyond GPT-J and Vicuna-7B.
Study how MeLLo works with smaller models such as GPT-2.
Improve MeLLo to require less manual prompt engineering.
papers.abstract: The information stored in large language models (LLMs) falls out of date quickly, and retraining from scratch is often not an option. This has recently given rise to a range of techniques for injecting new facts through updating model weights. Current evaluation paradigms are extremely limited, mainly validating the recall of edited facts, but changing one fact should cause rippling changes to the model's related beliefs. If we edit the UK Prime Minister to now be Rishi Sunak, then we should get a different answer to Who is married to the British Prime Minister? In this work, we present a benchmark MQuAKE (Multi-hop Question Answering for Knowledge Editing) comprising multi-hop questions that assess whether edited models correctly answer questions where the answer should change as an entailed consequence of edited facts. While we find that current knowledge-editing approaches can recall edited facts accurately, they fail catastrophically on the constructed multi-hop questions. We thus propose a simple memory-based approach, MeLLo, which stores all edited facts externally while prompting the language model iteratively to generate answers that are consistent with the edited facts. While MQuAKE remains challenging, we show that MeLLo scales well with LLMs (up to 175B) and outperforms previous model editors by a large margin.

papers.title: K-Edit: Language Model Editing with Contextual Knowledge Awareness
papers.research_question: How can knowledge-based model editing be improved to produce edits that account for associated contextual information and ensure consistency in multi-hop reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: K-Edit is a direct model editing algorithm that leverages knowledge graphs to generate contextual edits, improving multi-hop reasoning and consistency without degrading standard edit metrics or scalability.
papers.conclusion: K-Edit effectively improves contextual knowledge integration in model editing, enhancing multi-hop reasoning while maintaining scalability and edit quality.
papers.key_findings:
K-Edit significantly improves multi-hop question answering accuracy over edited information compared to baselines like MEMIT and ROME.
The method maintains high edit quality on standard metrics such as efficacy, paraphrase, and specificity, even when scaling to thousands of edits.
K-Edit shows generalization, where improvements extend to multi-hop edges not directly covered by contextual edits.
Sequential ordering of edits is crucial for performance, with parallel updates leading to decreased accuracy.
Performance declines with increasing number of edits and hops, but K-Edit handles this better than baselines.
papers.limitation:
Limited to adding context from a single additional hop and only in the forward direction.
Experiments are limited to English datasets and 7 billion parameter models.
future_direction: Extending K-Edit to broader and deeper contexts, including more relation types and increasing hop depth.
Incorporating contextual edges connected to the edit subject in addition to the target object.
Studying counterfactual knowledge tracing and better measures of contextual knowledge in edited representations.
papers.abstract: As the world changes, we need to be able to update our models and correct false information without costly retraining. Knowledge-based model editing enables precise modifications to the weights of large language models in order to modify the information encoded within. Recent approaches have seen success in enabling recall of edited information for thousands of edits at once. However, these approaches fail to produce edits that account for associated contextual information. We present K-Edit, an effective approach to generating contextually consistent knowledge edits. By using knowledge graphs, which maintain contextual consistency when an edge is edited, we are able to generate additional \textit{contextual edits} that ensure consistency of related information in the language model. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in multi-hop question answering while maintaining the general effectiveness and scalability of model edits.

papers.title: KnowledgeSmith: Uncovering Knowledge Updating in LLMs with Model Editing and Unlearning
papers.research_question: How does knowledge updating (via editing and unlearning) work in LLMs, including propagation, plasticity, consistency, and robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes KnowledgeSmith, a unified framework for understanding knowledge updating in LLMs via editing and unlearning, and provides insights into propagation asymmetry, plasticity scaling, consistency-capacity trade-off, and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents KnowledgeSmith, a unified framework for analyzing knowledge updating in LLMs, and reveals important trade-offs in propagation, plasticity, consistency, and robustness, offering insights for designing reliable updating strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Editing tends to over-spread (unintentionally altering related nodes), while unlearning under-spreads (failing to propagate beyond the target).
Smaller models exhibit higher immediate plasticity but are less stable; larger models require more data but are more consistent.
Increasing data can trigger consistency collapse, where local updates contradict other knowledge.
Editing improves in-domain accuracy but harms out-of-domain and adversarial stability, while unlearning preserves global robustness.
Editing balances integration and preservation with strong low-data efficiency, unlearning is conservative but stable, while LoRA fine-tuning is unstable.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing and machine unlearning are two popular approaches for large language models (LLMs) to stay up-to-date. However, the knowledge updating mechanism of LLMs remains largely unexplored due to insufficient, isolated, and small-scale evaluation. For instance, are LLMs similar to humans in modifying certain knowledge? What differs editing and unlearning as training data increases? This paper proposes KnowledgeSmith, a unified framework to systematically understand the updating mechanism of LLMs. We first cast editing and unlearning as instances of one constrained optimization problem. Then, we propose an automatic dataset generator that provides structured interventions across multiple graph levels and data scales, enabling controlled studies of how different modification strategies propagate through model knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate nuanced insights over knowledge propagation, plasticity scaling, consistency, and robustness. For instance, our results show that LLMs do not exhibit similar updating as humans for different levels of knowledge, and there exists consistency-capacity trade-off. We hope our findings can offer suggestions to the design of more reliable and scalable strategies. Code: https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/KnowledgeSmith.git

papers.title: Stable Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we perform stable knowledge editing in large language models, overcoming the instability caused by assumptions of localized and isolated knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces StableKE, a knowledge editing method based on knowledge augmentation (Semantic Paraphrase Enhancement and Contextual Description Enrichment) rather than knowledge localization, which demonstrates superior stability across edited knowledge, multi-hop knowledge, unrelated knowledge, and general abilities.
papers.conclusion: StableKE is a simple yet effective method for editing knowledge in LLMs, demonstrating that the quality of data used for augmentation is more crucial than the editing structure itself for achieving stable edits.
papers.key_findings:
StableKE outperforms previous knowledge editing methods (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, MEND, SERAC) across four stability dimensions, especially in large-scale batch and sequential editing settings.
The method maintains the model's instruction-following and chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities after editing.
Increasing the number of semantic paraphrases (Kspe) improves edited knowledge stability, with performance plateauing after a certain point.
StableKE can be effectively applied using different fine-tuning approaches, including full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA.
The method is also effective for editing knowledge in closed-source models like ChatGPT via their fine-tuning API.
papers.limitation: Despite StableKE exhibiting stability across various knowledge editing settings, its overall performance exhibits a downward trend in a sequential editing setting.
papers.abstract: Efficient knowledge editing of large language models is crucial for replacing obsolete information or incorporating specialized knowledge on a large scale. However, previous methods implicitly assume that knowledge is localized and isolated within the model, an assumption that oversimplifies the interconnected nature of model knowledge. The premise of localization results in an incomplete knowledge editing, whereas an isolated assumption may impair both other knowledge and general abilities. It introduces instability to the performance of the knowledge editing method. To transcend these assumptions, we introduce StableKE, a method adopts a novel perspective based on knowledge augmentation rather than knowledge localization. To overcome the expense of human labeling, StableKE integrates two automated knowledge augmentation strategies: Semantic Paraphrase Enhancement strategy, which diversifies knowledge descriptions to facilitate the teaching of new information to the model, and Contextual Description Enrichment strategy, expanding the surrounding knowledge to prevent the forgetting of related information. StableKE surpasses other knowledge editing methods, demonstrating stability both edited knowledge and multi-hop knowledge, while also preserving unrelated knowledge and general abilities. Moreover, StableKE can edit knowledge on ChatGPT.

papers.title: Revealing and Mitigating Over-Attention in Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: What causes specificity failure in knowledge editing, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies attention drift as the primary cause of specificity failure in knowledge editing and proposes SADR, a regularization method that constrains attention weight changes during editing to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention drift is a key issue in knowledge editing and that SADR effectively mitigates specificity failure without compromising edit success.
papers.key_findings:
Specificity failure in knowledge editing is primarily caused by attention drift, where attention heads overly focus on the edited subject.
Patching attention drift can significantly mitigate specificity failure.
The proposed SADR method effectively reduces specificity failure across multiple models and editing methods with minimal impact on edit success.
Attention drift is correlated with the probability of incorrect answers in specificity tasks.
The maximum attention drift on the edited subject token among heads is a primary trigger for specificity failure.
papers.limitation: Knowledge editing techniques can be misused to generate toxic and harmful content.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated superior performance across a wide range of tasks, but they still exhibit undesirable errors due to incorrect knowledge learned from the training data. To avoid this, knowledge editing methods emerged to precisely edit the specific model knowledge via efficiently modifying a very small percentage of parameters. % However, those methods can lead to the problem of Specificity Failure: when the content related to the edited knowledge occurs in the context, it can inadvertently corrupt other pre-existing knowledge. However, those methods can lead to the problem of Specificity Failure, where the existing knowledge and capabilities are severely degraded due to editing. Our preliminary indicates that Specificity Failure primarily stems from the model's attention heads assigning excessive attention scores to entities related to the edited knowledge, thereby unduly focusing on specific snippets within the context, which we denote as the Attention Drift phenomenon. To mitigate such Attention Drift issue, we introduce a simple yet effective method Selective Attention Drift Restriction}(SADR), which introduces an additional regularization term during the knowledge editing process to restrict changes in the attention weight distribution, thereby preventing undue focus on the edited entity. Experiments on five frequently used strong LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, where SADR can significantly mitigate Specificity Failure in the predominant knowledge editing tasks.

papers.title: Enhancing Semantic Consistency of Large Language Models through Model Editing: An Interpretability-Oriented Approach
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) through an interpretable model editing approach that identifies and modifies key internal components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a model editing method that identifies key attention heads and MLPs responsible for semantic inconsistency and injects biases into their activations, improving semantic consistency and task performance without mass parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The proposed model editing method effectively improves the semantic consistency and task performance of LLMs by targeting and modifying key internal components, while also demonstrating generalization to out-of-domain tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads and MLPs in the mid to final decoder blocks are highly relevant to an LLM's semantic consistency.
Injecting biases into the outputs of these key components significantly improves semantic consistency and task performance on NLU and NLG datasets.
The proposed editing method is computationally efficient, requiring up to 23 times fewer GPU hours than supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
The method shows promising generalization capabilities on out-of-domain tasks.
Excessive editing (too many components or too strong a bias) can degrade model performance.
papers.limitation:
Attention heads tend to have a more predominant influence than MLPs, and the role of MLPs in semantic consistency requires further exploration.
The editing method is not sufficiently validated in terms of other metrics like locality and portability.
The model editing method lags behind supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in terms of performance improvement.
future_direction: Explore the role of MLPs in the semantic consistency of LLMs.
Develop more rigorous and effective testing methods to evaluate the proposed method's locality and portability.
Extend research to identify circuits related to semantic consistency and understand their causal mechanisms.
papers.abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM) tends to generate inconsistent and sometimes contradictory outputs when presented with a prompt that has equivalent semantics but is expressed differently from the original prompt. To achieve semantic consistency of an LLM, one of the key approaches is to finetune the model with prompt-output pairs with semantically equivalent meanings. Despite its effectiveness, a data-driven finetuning method incurs substantial computation costs in data preparation and model optimization. In this regime, an LLM is treated as a ``black box'', restricting our ability to gain deeper insights into its internal mechanism. In this paper, we are motivated to enhance the semantic consistency of LLMs through a more interpretable method (i.e., model editing) to this end. We first identify the model components (i.e., attention heads) that have a key impact on the semantic consistency of an LLM. We subsequently inject biases into the output of these model components along the semantic-consistency activation direction. It is noteworthy that these modifications are cost-effective, without reliance on mass manipulations of the original model parameters. Through comprehensive experiments on the constructed NLU and open-source NLG datasets, our method demonstrates significant improvements in the semantic consistency and task performance of LLMs. Additionally, our method exhibits promising generalization capabilities by performing well on tasks beyond the primary tasks.

papers.title: CaKE: Circuit-aware Editing Enables Generalizable Knowledge Learners
papers.research_question: Why do current knowledge editing methods fail to generalize updated knowledge to multi-hop reasoning tasks, and how can this be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CaKE, a circuit-aware knowledge editing method that improves the integration of updated knowledge into reasoning circuits, enabling better generalization in multi-hop reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: CaKE aligns knowledge editing with the inherent reasoning architectures of LLMs, enabling generalizable multi-hop knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
Current knowledge editing methods like ROME and WISE fail in multi-hop reasoning due to misalignment with reasoning circuits.
CaKE outperforms existing methods on multi-hop benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in accuracy.
CaKE requires only a few curated data samples to integrate knowledge effectively.
CaKE maintains model locality and general ability while editing knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on factual knowledge and multi-hop reasoning, not other domains like math or long-form reasoning.
Does not deeply investigate fine-grained circuit components like relational information.
Connection between model abilities and training data is underexplored.
future_direction: Investigate knowledge editing in other reasoning domains such as long-form mathematics.
Explore enhancement of knowledge utilization in slow-thinking paradigms like chain-of-thought.
Develop more concise methods for knowledge editing focusing on fine-grained circuit components.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) enables the modification of outdated or incorrect information in large language models (LLMs). While existing KE methods can update isolated facts, they often fail to generalize these updates to multi-hop reasoning tasks that rely on the modified knowledge. Through an analysis of reasoning circuits -- the neural pathways LLMs use for knowledge-based inference, we find that current layer-localized KE approaches (e.g., MEMIT, WISE), which edit only single or a few model layers, inadequately integrate updated knowledge into these reasoning pathways. To address this limitation, we present CaKE (Circuit-aware Knowledge Editing), a novel method that enhances the effective integration of updated knowledge in LLMs. By only leveraging a few curated data samples guided by our circuit-based analysis, CaKE stimulates the model to develop appropriate reasoning circuits for newly incorporated knowledge. Experiments show that CaKE enables more accurate and consistent use of edited knowledge across related reasoning tasks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in multi-hop reasoning accuracy on the MQuAKE dataset while requiring less memory than existing KE methods. We release the code and data in https://github.com/zjunlp/CaKE.

papers.title: Bilinear relational structure fixes reversal curse and enables consistent model editing
papers.research_question: Is the reversal curse an inherent limitation of language models, and can it be mitigated by learning a bilinear relational structure in internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The reversal curse and model editing failures are not inherent but stem from unstructured knowledge representations; training with appropriate regularization induces a bilinear relational structure that mitigates the curse and enables logically consistent editing.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse and editing generalization failures are symptoms of unstructured internal knowledge representations; inducing bilinear relational geometry through training and regularization leads to more reliable and editable language models.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay regularization enables models to overcome the reversal curse by learning a more generalizable internal structure.
Successful models develop a robust bilinear relational structure in their hidden representations, peaking in middle layers.
The learned bilinear matrices obey algebraic properties (inversion via transpose, composition via product), enabling multi-hop inference.
Models with bilinear structure successfully propagate single-fact edits to logically entailed facts (reverse and neighborhood relations).
A strong positive correlation exists between a model's bilinear probe accuracy and its logical generalization performance after editing.
papers.limitation: The study uses language models trained from scratch on a clean, synthetic dataset, which may not scale to large, pre-trained language models with noisy, complex knowledge.
future_direction: Investigate whether similar bilinear structures exist in large-scale pre-trained language models.
Develop geometry-aware editing algorithms that leverage internal relational structures.
Explore 'architectural preparation' strategies to endow models with structured knowledge representations during pre-training or fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The reversal curse -- a language model's (LM) inability to infer an unseen fact ``B is A'' from a learned fact ``A is B'' -- is widely considered a fundamental limitation. We show that this is not an inherent failure but an artifact of how models encode knowledge. By training LMs from scratch on a synthetic dataset of relational knowledge graphs, we demonstrate that bilinear relational structure emerges in their hidden representations. This structure substantially alleviates the reversal curse, enabling LMs to infer unseen reverse facts. Crucially, we also find that this bilinear structure plays a key role in consistent model editing. When a fact is updated in a LM with this structure, the edit correctly propagates to its reverse and other logically dependent facts. In contrast, models lacking this representation not only suffer from the reversal curse but also fail to generalize edits, further introducing logical inconsistencies. Our results establish that training on a relational knowledge dataset induces the emergence of bilinear internal representations, which in turn enable LMs to behave in a logically consistent manner after editing. This implies that the success of model editing depends critically not just on editing algorithms but on the underlying representational geometry of the knowledge being modified.

papers.title: Evaluating Dependencies in Fact Editing for Language Models: Specificity and Implication Awareness
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how well existing knowledge editing methods for language models respect dependency constraints, specifically whether they can edit facts without affecting irrelevant ones (specificity) and whether they can correctly infer logical implications of edited facts (implication awareness).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new evaluation protocol (establish-and-update) and dataset (DepEdit) for assessing knowledge editing methods in language models with respect to dependency constraints (specificity and implication awareness), and finds that existing methods are sensitive to surface form and perform poorly on implication awareness.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current knowledge editing methods are limited in handling dependency constraints, especially implication awareness, and suggests that future work should develop methods that better incorporate logical dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (MEND, MEMIT) are sensitive to lexical variations and perform worse when questions are rephrased.
These methods struggle to update logical implications of edited facts, treating implications as unrelated knowledge.
Fine-tuning achieves high success rates but disrupts unrelated facts, while MEND and MEMIT better preserve unrelated facts.
Gradient similarity between updating premise facts and implications is low, similar to that between facts with similar surface forms.
External inference mechanisms (forward/backward chaining) can improve implication editing but may introduce inconsistencies.
papers.limitation:
DepEdit does not support evaluation of knowledge editing with complex logical operations such as quantification and probabilistic entailment.
Each knowledge set contains only one rule and avoids conflicts among facts and implications, which may not reflect real-world scenarios.
future_direction: Develop implication-aware knowledge editing methods inspired by knowledge base editing techniques.
Extend DepEdit to include multiple rules per knowledge set and handle conflicts.
Extend DepEdit to support complex logical operations like quantification and probabilistic entailment.
papers.abstract: The potential of using a large language model (LLM) as a knowledge base (KB) has sparked significant interest. To manage the knowledge acquired by LLMs, we need to ensure that the editing of learned facts respects internal logical constraints, which are known as dependency of knowledge. Existing work on editing LLMs has partially addressed the issue of dependency, when the editing of a fact should apply to its lexical variations without disrupting irrelevant ones. However, they neglect the dependency between a fact and its logical implications. We propose an evaluation protocol with an accompanying question-answering dataset, DepEdit, that provides a comprehensive assessment of the editing process considering the above notions of dependency. Our protocol involves setting up a controlled environment in which we edit facts and monitor their impact on LLMs, along with their implications based on If-Then rules. Extensive experiments on DepEdit show that existing knowledge editing methods are sensitive to the surface form of knowledge, and that they have limited performance in inferring the implications of edited facts.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Lifelong Knowledge Editing requires Better Regularization
papers.research_question: What causes model degradation during sequential knowledge editing, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies over-optimization of activations and norm-growth of edited matrices as causes of model degradation in sequential knowledge editing, and introduces MPES and Frobenius norm-constraint to mitigate these issues.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that targeted regularization is essential for lifelong knowledge editing, and the combination of MPES and norm-constraint allows for scalable editing without significant model degradation.
papers.key_findings:
Over-optimization of target activations during gradient-descent leads to edited facts being predicted with abnormally high confidence.
Sequential editing causes continuous norm growth of edited MLP matrices, which dominates the residual stream and harms downstream performance.
MPES stops gradient-descent when edited facts become most probable, reducing over-optimization and improving editing speed by 42-61%.
Adding a Frobenius norm-constraint to the editing objective controls norm growth and helps preserve downstream task performance.
Combining MPES and norm-constraint enables scaling to 10,000 sequential edits while maintaining original downstream performance.
papers.limitation: Scaling beyond 10,000 edits is challenging due to compute constraints, and larger-scale comparisons are infeasible with slower baseline methods.
future_direction: Explore more efficient optimization techniques or hardware acceleration to push beyond the current edit limit.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing is a promising way to improve factuality in large language models, but recent studies have shown significant model degradation during sequential editing. In this paper, we formalize the popular locate-then-edit methods as a two-step fine-tuning process, allowing us to precisely identify the root cause of this degradation. We show that model degradation occurs due to (1) over-optimization of internal activations and (2) continuous norm-growth of edited matrices. To mitigate these issues, we introduce two regularization techniques: (1) Most-Probable Early Stopping (MPES) and (2) explicit Frobenius norm-constraint. We demonstrate that applying these simple yet effective regularization techniques at key points in the editing process can substantially mitigate model degradation. Combining these regularization methods enables scaling locate-then-edit methods to 10,000 edits while reducing editing time by 42-61%. These results show that targeted regularization is essential for lifelong knowledge editing.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: See the Unseen: Better Context-Consistent Knowledge-Editing by Noises
papers.research_question: How can we edit LLMs’ knowledge while maintaining the knowledge can be applied in context-consistency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that FFN activations for knowledge-related tokens are context-consistent and follow a Gaussian-like distribution, and proposes a noise-based editing method that improves generalization by simulating unseen contexts.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that deep noise editing, motivated by the Gaussian-like distribution of context shifts in FFN activations, significantly improves the generalization of knowledge editing in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
FFN activations for knowledge-related tokens are context-consistent and their shifts across different contexts follow a narrow Gaussian-like distribution.
Attention scopes do not differ significantly between knowledge-related tokens and control tokens.
FFNs exhibit particular behavior for knowledge tokens across all layers, even the first layer.
Adding Gaussian noises to FFN activations during editing (deep noise editing) improves generalization to unseen contexts.
The proposed method works on different transformer-based LLMs (GPT2-xl, GPT-J, LLaMA-2) and outperforms other noise-based fine-tuning methods in knowledge editing.
papers.limitation:
Due to incomplete open-sources and limited computing resources, experiments do not include editing larger LLMs or editing multiple cases with Counterfacts on LLaMA-2.
Following fixed hyperparameter settings may not yield optimal results for the proposed method and baselines.
papers.abstract: Knowledge-editing updates knowledge of large language models (LLMs) and contributes to the interpretability and application of LLMs. However, knowledge applying is context-consistent: LLMs can recall the same knowledge in different contexts. Existing works ignore this property and the editing lacks generalization. In this paper, we empirically find that the effects of different contexts upon LLMs in recalling the same knowledge follow a Gaussian-like distribution. We then sample Gaussian noises to simulate the effects of different contexts when updating LLMs. By such, we can make LLMs see the unseen contexts where the edited knowledge will be applied, therefore improving the editing generalization. Experimental results on three LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods and also distinguish our methods from the others of fine-tuning LLMs by noises.

papers.title: Latent Knowledge Scalpel: Precise and Massive Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enable precise and large-scale knowledge editing for large language models without compromising their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Latent Knowledge Scalpel (LKS), an LLM editor that uses a lightweight hyper-network to manipulate entity latent knowledge for precise and large-scale editing while preserving general abilities.
papers.conclusion: LKS enables precise and scalable knowledge editing in LLMs, highlighting the structured nature of entity representations and opening new possibilities for efficient updates.
papers.key_findings:
LKS outperforms other model editing methods in reliability, generality, and locality.
LKS can perform up to 10,000 simultaneous edits effectively.
LKS preserves the general abilities of LLMs, such as mathematical reasoning and sentiment analysis, even after large-scale editing.
Entity knowledge blocks in LLMs contain semantic information and internal representations retain syntactic structure.
Modifying intermediate layers yields higher effectiveness for knowledge editing.
papers.limitation: The Edit Scope Indicator incurs overhead by identifying entities, which can be mitigated by optimizing the entity recognition mechanism.
future_direction: Optimizing the entity recognition mechanism, e.g., by incorporating vector-level semantic matching or building an entity alias dictionary.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often retain inaccurate or outdated information from pre-training, leading to incorrect predictions or biased outputs during inference. While existing model editing methods can address this challenge, they struggle with editing large amounts of factual information simultaneously and may compromise the general capabilities of the models. In this paper, our empirical study demonstrates that it is feasible to edit the internal representations of LLMs and replace the entities in a manner similar to editing natural language inputs. Based on this insight, we introduce the Latent Knowledge Scalpel (LKS), an LLM editor that manipulates the latent knowledge of specific entities via a lightweight hypernetwork to enable precise and large-scale editing. Experiments conducted on Llama-2 and Mistral show even with the number of simultaneous edits reaching 10,000, LKS effectively performs knowledge editing while preserving the general abilities of the edited LLMs. Code is available at: https://github.com/Linuxin-xxx/LKS.

papers.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs genuinely believe facts implanted via knowledge editing techniques, and develops a framework to measure the depth of such beliefs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to measure belief depth in LLMs for implanted facts, operationalized through generality, robustness, and internal representations. It finds that Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often implants beliefs deeply, while prompting and mechanistic editing fail.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that measuring belief depth is crucial for evaluating knowledge editing, and while SDF can implant deep beliefs, its effectiveness varies with fact plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting and mechanistic editing fail to implant knowledge deeply; beliefs are not robust and have internal representations distinct from genuine knowledge.
Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often succeeds in implanting beliefs that generalize to related contexts, are robust to scrutiny, and have similar internal representations to genuine knowledge.
SDF's success depends on fact plausibility; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
Implanted beliefs from SDF are robust to increased inference-time compute, with minimal impact on belief rates.
Internal representations of SDF-implanted facts resemble genuine knowledge for plausible facts, but adversarial probes can distinguish implausible ones.
papers.limitation: SDF's success is not universal; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
future_direction: Continued evaluation of SDF on highly capable future systems
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing techniques promise to implant new factual knowledge into large language models (LLMs). But do LLMs really believe these facts? We develop a framework to measure belief depth and use it to evaluate the success of knowledge editing techniques. We operationalize belief depth as the extent to which implanted knowledge 1) generalizes to related contexts (e.g. Fermi estimates several logical steps removed), 2) is robust to self-scrutiny and direct challenge, and 3) is represented similarly to genuine knowledge (as measured by linear probes). Our evaluations show that simple prompting and mechanistic editing techniques fail to implant knowledge deeply. In contrast, Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) - where models are trained on LLM-generated documents consistent with a fact - often succeeds at implanting beliefs that behave similarly to genuine knowledge. However, SDF's success is not universal, as implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct from genuine knowledge. Overall, our work introduces measurable criteria for belief depth and enables the rigorous evaluation necessary for deploying knowledge editing in real-world applications.

papers.title: EVEDIT: Event-based Knowledge Editing for Deterministic Knowledge Propagation
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in large language models be improved to reduce uncertainty and enable confident knowledge propagation by addressing the issue of undefined deduction anchors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces event-based knowledge editing to reduce uncertainty in knowledge propagation, proposes the EVEDIT benchmark, and presents the Self-Edit method which improves consistency while maintaining naturalness.
papers.conclusion: Event-based knowledge editing provides a more robust and practical setting for knowledge editing, and the Self-Edit method effectively improves consistency while preserving naturalness.
